---
format:
  revealjs:
    theme:
      - default
      - assets/theme.scss
    width: 1600
    height: 900
    # Figure-heavy science talks that need a text column beside a large figure
    # often read better on a wider canvas. To use ~21:9, set:
    #   width: 2100
    # and scale figure base_size / linewidths up to match (see the setup chunk).
    center: false
    slide-number: c/t
    hash: true
    menu: true
    progress: true
    controls: true
    transition: fade
    embed-resources: true
execute:
  echo: false
  warning: false
  message: false
params:
  config_file: "presentation.yml"
  project_root: "."
---

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
# Keep embedded figures light so the self-contained HTML stays small: render
# inline figures at screen (1x) resolution. Pre-optimize any external images
# into an `optimized/` folder before embedding them (see README "File size").
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  dev = "png",
  dev.args = list(bg = "transparent"),
  dpi = 96,
  fig.retina = 1
)
source("R/presentation_helpers.R")
if (requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)) {
  ggplot2::theme_set(presentation_theme())
}
cfg <- read_presentation_config(params$config_file, params$project_root)
validate_presentation_inputs(cfg)
summary_object <- load_presentation_summary(cfg)
spict <- if (identical(cfg$data$adapter, "spict")) {
  extract_spict_context(summary_object)
} else {
  NULL
}
```

## Trajectories should carry the argument {data-section="Results"}

:::: {.text-figure}
::: {.text-panel}
- Put the interpretation beside the visual when the audience needs guidance.
- Keep the text short enough that the figure remains the dominant proof object.

::: {.takeaway}
Use `.text-figure` for concise bullets on the left and a figure on the right.
:::
:::

::: {.figure-panel}
```{r}
#| label: plot-spict-trajectories
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| out-width: 100%
plot_spict_trajectories(spict)
```
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Charts should be generated from the compact result object. Use the analysis
project for complex plotting functions and call those functions here when
possible.
:::

## Choose a layout by proof object {data-section="Style sampler"}

:::: {.grid-3}
::: {.card}
::: {.card-title}
`.grid-2` / `.grid-3`
:::

Use cards when the proof object is a small set of comparable concepts.
:::

::: {.card}
::: {.card-title}
`.metric-grid`
:::

Use metric cards for repeated indicators with a shared interpretation.
:::

::: {.card}
::: {.card-title}
`.table-slide`
:::

Use narrow tables when exact scenario values matter more than shape.
:::
::::

::: {.takeaway}
Pick the layout from the evidence type first, then write the slide claim.
:::

::: {.notes}
This sampler slide is meant to make the reusable classes visible in the
starter deck. Delete it from project decks after selecting the relevant
patterns.
:::

## Diagnostic cards keep technical checks legible {data-section="Style sampler"}

:::: {.diagnostic-grid}
::: {.diagnostic-card}
::: {.diagnostic-number}
1
:::
::: {.card-title}
Fit
:::

Show whether observations and fitted values disagree systematically.
:::

::: {.diagnostic-card}
::: {.diagnostic-number}
2
:::
::: {.card-title}
Stability
:::

Show whether derived quantities change when data, years, or assumptions move.
:::
::::

::: {.small-note}
Use `.diagnostic-grid` for a short map of checks before showing dense
diagnostic figures.
:::

::: {.notes}
This style works well before residual, retrospective, sensitivity, or
comparison plots.
:::

## Emphasis styles separate caveats from conclusions {data-section="Style sampler"}

::: {.alert-box}
Use `.alert-box` for a caveat, risk, or modelling limitation that should not be
missed.
:::

:::: {.takeaway-grid}
::: {.takeaway-card}
::: {.card-title}
Finding
:::

The evidence supports one clear statement.
:::

::: {.takeaway-card}
::: {.card-title}
Caveat
:::

The result has one important boundary.
:::

::: {.takeaway-card}
::: {.card-title}
Next step
:::

The audience knows what to do with the result.
:::
::::

::: {.deadline}
Use `.deadline` for review dates, decision points, or meeting constraints.
:::

::: {.closing}
Use `.closing` for a short final line.
:::

::: {.notes}
Use emphasis styles sparingly. They are strongest when the rest of the slide is
quiet.
:::

## A wrapped title can sit beside a full-height figure {.bleed-figure-slide data-section="Style sampler"}

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="40%"}

- Put the interpretation in a narrow column on the left.
- Reveal bullets one at a time when the audience needs to follow a chain of
  reasoning.

::: {.fragment}
- A `.fragment` appears on the next click.
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.takeaway}
Pair RevealJS `.columns` with an `.absolute` figure in the wide column when one
chart or map must dominate the slide.
:::
:::

:::

::: {.column width="60%" .add-space}
::: {.absolute top=-150 right=-100 height=1000}
```{r}
#| label: plot-bleed-figure-demo
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 6
#| out-height: 1000px
plot_spict_trajectories(spict)
```
:::
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
On a figure-heavy science slide, a narrow text column beside a large `.absolute`
figure usually reads better than a balanced two-column grid. This mirrors the
manual `ref-index` pattern: constrain the title width, put bullets in the left
column, and place the dominant figure with `top=-150 right=-100 height=1000`.
On a wide (~21:9) canvas the figure can extend close to the slide edge. Use
fragments to pace the argument, and keep the figure the dominant proof object.
:::

## Swap two figures in the same spot {data-section="Style sampler"}

::: {.r-stack}

::: {.fragment .fade-out fragment-index=1}
```{r}
#| label: plot-swap-a
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| out-width: 100%
plot_spict_trajectories(spict)
```
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in fragment-index=1}
```{r}
#| label: plot-swap-b
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| out-width: 100%
plot_spict_trajectories(spict)
```
:::

:::

::: {.small-note}
Stack figures in a `.r-stack` and pair `.fade-out` / `.fade-in` on the same
`fragment-index` to swap one figure for another in place — useful for comparing
two species, scenarios, or model variants without moving the audience's eye.
:::

::: {.notes}
Both panels here draw the same placeholder; in a real deck the two chunks would
plot different objects. Use `.fade-in-then-out` for the middle steps of a longer
sequence so each figure appears, then clears for the next.
:::

## Tables can share a slide with a compact figure {data-section="Style sampler"}

```{r}
#| label: table-style-sampler
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    Scenario = c("Reference", "Lower catch", "Higher catch"),
    `Catch (t)` = c("TBD", "TBD", "TBD"),
    `Risk` = c("TBD", "TBD", "TBD"),
    check.names = FALSE
  ),
  align = c("l", "r", "r")
)
```

::: {.scenario-figure}
```{r}
#| label: plot-style-sampler
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 2.7
#| out-width: 100%
old_par <- par(no.readonly = TRUE)
par(mar = c(2.5, 3.2, 0.4, 0.4), mgp = c(1.8, 0.6, 0))
plot(
  1:6,
  c(2.1, 2.4, 2.2, 2.8, 3.0, 3.2),
  type = "b",
  lwd = 3,
  pch = 19,
  col = "#056A89",
  xlab = "Step",
  ylab = "Relative value"
)
par(old_par)
```
:::

::: {.notes}
Use `.scenario-figure` when a narrow table needs a small visual check beneath
it. Keep the figure compact so the table remains readable.
:::

## Compare scenarios in one table {data-section="Results"}

```{r}
#| label: scenario-table
knitr::kable(
  scenario_table(spict),
  align = c("l", "r", "r", "r")
)
```

::: {.takeaway}
State the decision-facing comparison in one sentence.
:::

::: {.notes}
Keep tables narrow enough to read from the back of the room. Put the full
scenario table in an appendix if more columns are needed.
:::

:::: {.takeaway-grid}
::: {.takeaway-card}
::: {.card-title}
Finding
:::

::: {.card-title}
